transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 39 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng), Maya Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Marta Alvarez (CTO, Nereid), Ethan Gray (Platform Eng), Priya Saini (SRE), Damien Huo (Product)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Nereid evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for LLM inference on routing/search and summarization features.
- Main constraints: monthly token budget cap (~$40k net), 99th pctl latency target of ~250ms for short chat flows, and SOC2 + KMS requirements for PII.
- Redwood to propose pilot scope, run dedicated throughput benchmark, and share compliance artifacts.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching and prefix cache levers, residency and private deployment constraints, pilot scope and benchmarking, security requirements

Key action items: see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining on a friday afternoon, really appreciate it. quick roll call?
[00:08] Marta Alvarez: hi, i'm marta, cto at nereid. thanks for taking the time.
[00:11] Ethan Gray: ethan here, platform. we're trying to decide hosting path for inference.
[00:16] Alex Chen: alex from redwood se, excited to dig into your workloads.
[00:19] Priya Saini: priya, sre. mainly worried about consistency and key management.
[00:23] Jordan Lee: jordan, i'll cover runtime-level questions and batching behavior.
[00:26] Samir Patel: great. quick agenda: 1) you walk us through where you're at and constraints, 2) we map hosting options to unit economics and levers, and 3) agree next steps. sound ok?
[00:33] Damien Huo: yep that's perfect.

[00:45] Marta Alvarez: so high level — we power a route optimization assistant and an in-app summarizer for drivers. call volume peaks 9–11am and 4–6pm local, so we need predictable capacity.
[00:57] Ethan Gray: average request payloads are short, 120–300 tokens, but we also have longer summarization jobs 2–4k tokens maybe a few hundred times a day.
[01:09] Samir Patel: good, that's the mixed profile we see a lot. what's the monthly spend you have in mind? i think you mentioned a cap?
[01:16] Marta Alvarez: roughly $40k a month for inference if possible. would prefer to keep it below that as we test.
[01:22] Alex Chen: ok. quick mapping — Hosted is simplest: pay-as-you-go per-token, auto-scaling; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput (lower per-token cost at scale), and Private adds VPC + KMS for data residency and fully private control plane.
[01:36] Priya Saini: for us security is non-negotiable. we need KMS integration, audit logs, and probably SOC2 evidence. can hosted satisfy that or do we need private?
[01:45] Samir Patel: hosted supports KMS envelope encryption and we provide audit logs and SOC2 attestation, but some customers prefer Private for full control of the control plane and customer-managed KMS. it's really about the policy and procurement appetite.
[01:58] Marta Alvarez: procurement will push for private if there's any doubt. also latency — we target 99th pct under 250ms for the short chat flow. hosted jitter historically — is that problematic?
[02:10] Jordan Lee: short flows of 120–300 tokens are very sensitive to batching behavior. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching; we try to keep the batching window small on low-latency tiers. with Dedicated you can reserve capacity so batching windows stay tight and you avoid cold start jitter. hosted can hit that target for most customers but if you need hard SLOs, Dedicated or Private gives more control.
[02:32] Ethan Gray: curious about numbers — what's per-token price delta between hosted and dedicated? any example scenarios?
[02:38] Samir Patel: sure — rough examples (ballpark): hosted generation could be $0.0009 per token for the model you mentioned; Dedicated reserved slots can drop that unit cost by 25–40% depending on commit and utilization. caching/prefix KV and quantization also change effective unit cost.
[02:52] Damien Huo: can you unpack caching and kv? is that something we control?
[02:55] Alex Chen: yes — so two levers: prefix caching and KV cache reuse. for route optimization we can cache common prefixes — that reduces new token generation. also for chat flows we keep kv caches warm for sessions, which avoids re-computing past context. Redwood Optimize can suggest batch sizes and cache TTLs based on your actual distribution. both levers reduce billed generation tokens.
[03:18] Priya Saini: is cached output billed? i.e., if we serve a cached response are tokens billed?
[03:22] Samir Patel: good question— we bill for tokens generated by the model. if a response is fully served from a cache layer with no model generation, there are no gen tokens billed. partial cache hits reduce effective tokens.
[03:32] Marta Alvarez: that could be huge for us — a lot of our queries are templated.

[03:45] Ethan Gray: what about batching — does higher batch size always reduce costs? what's the latency tradeoff?
[03:49] Jordan Lee: batching increases throughput and amortizes per-inference overhead, so cost per token falls. but latency increases with batch queuing time. Redwood supports workload-aware batching where we set max latency SLO and the runtime dynamically forms batches that meet it. On Dedicated, with steady load, you can size nodes to keep batch latency minimal while still getting cost benefits.
[04:10] Alex Chen: also worth noting tokenization differences — some prompts tokenise into more tokens than expected; we usually run a tokenization audit as part of the pilot so you have realistic burn numbers.

[04:28] Ethan Gray: do you have an example pilot scope for our workload? like what you would run to give us real per-token numbers?
[04:34] Samir Patel: typical pilot: 2–4 week POC, run in Dedicated (or hosted if you prefer) with two parts: 1) synthetic traffic that mimics peak profile to measure throughput/latency; 2) live shadow traffic for a subset of queries to measure real token distribution and cache hit rates. we then produce a model per-token/latency/cost projection.
[04:56] Marta Alvarez: budget wise — if dedicated gives lower unit cost but requires commit, how should we think about commit size vs expected usage?
[05:03] Alex Chen: commits are negotiable — we can model break-even points. e.g., if you commit to a reserved pool that covers 70% of peak, your blended per-token can be 30% lower; if you underutilize you'll still pay for reserved capacity so we recommend conservative ramp-up pilots. we can create a utilization sensitivity sheet for you.

[05:25] Damien Huo: any pitfalls with quantization? we rely on high-quality outputs for summarization and routing — don't want hallucinations.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: quantization often trades a small amount of output fidelity for big perf gains. we have model-specific recommendations and run quality regressions on your eval set during the pilot. for summaries we can pin model variants and run A/B tests.

[05:46] Priya Saini: on KMS — do you support customer-managed keys and HSM? logs must show access to models and data flows for audits.
[05:54] Samir Patel: yes — Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and stores audit logs you can ship to your SIEM. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer keys in many cases but Private is for fully air-gapped/network-isolated scenarios.

[06:10] Marta Alvarez: procurement also asked about data residency — we have some EU customers; is region pinning possible?
[06:15] Alex Chen: absolutely — Hosted can pin region, Dedicated pools are regional, and Private gives you full control over which datacenter/region the inference runs in.

[06:25] Ethan Gray: ok can we talk numbers again — you gave a hosted example of $0.0009/token — what assumptions are behind that?
[06:31] Samir Patel: that's for a medium-size open model at default precision for generation. it assumes standard batching, no prefix caching, and moderate concurrency. If you enable prefix cache for templated queries and reuse kv caches for sessions, your effective per-interaction token cost can drop 20–60% depending on hit rates.

[06:50] Damien Huo: what's the cost to run the long summarization jobs — 2–4k tokens — is there a separate pricing or is it same per-token?
[06:56] Samir Patel: same per-token billing; however longer sequences affect memory and throughput. For large off-peak batch summarizations we often suggest running them on lower-cost reserved capacity or scheduled batch jobs to avoid interrupting low-latency traffic. That keeps unit economics healthy.

[07:12] Priya Saini: for our SLOs we need a clear fall-back if dedicated capacity hits a spike offload pattern — do you do automatic fallback to hosted variants?
[07:20] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood can set routing policies: primary Dedicated, fallback to hosted compatible variants, and you can configure graceful degradation like lower context window or smaller model for non-critical paths. We also have cost-aware routing if you want to cap spend.

[07:34] Marta Alvarez: anything else we should be aware of with CPU vs GPU mix? we've experimented with CPU-based embeddings and cheaper CPUs for low-priority jobs.
[07:41] Jordan Lee: embeddings are often cheaper on CPU at lower performance needs. Redwood can route embeddings to CPU pools and generation to GPU; that mixed strategy helps control costs.

[07:50] Ethan Gray: what about concurrency targets? we're planning a burst to 400 qps at peak across routes — can dedicated handle that?
[07:57] Alex Chen: depends on model and sequence length; Dedicated with autoscale and burst capacity can handle 400 qps if sized properly. part of the pilot benchmark will validate that.

[08:10] Samir Patel: quick follow-up on procurement timelines — when do you expect to decide?
[08:14] Marta Alvarez: procurement timeline is ~6 weeks but technical eval needs to happen first. if pilot looks good, legal procurement usually takes the rest.

[08:23] Damien Huo: are there any hidden fees like egress or storage we should watch?
[08:27] Samir Patel: standard cloud egress applies for Private if you host in your VPC; for Hosted we include model storage and token billing but large artifact egress can be discussed. We'll outline these in the pricing sheet.

[08:38] Ethan Gray: ok can we go through an example billing calc for a sample day? say 50k short-chat requests (200 tokens average) + 300 summarization jobs (3k tokens avg).
[08:50] Samir Patel: sure quick calc: short chat: 50k * 200 = 10M tokens; summaries: 300 * 3k = 900k tokens; total 10.9M tokens/day. at $0.0009/token hosted = $9,810/day ~ $294k/mo — which is over your $40k target. But this is naive: with caching and batching and dedicated pricing the numbers shift a lot. if caching hits reduce generated tokens by 40%, and dedicated drop is 30% on unit price, effective monthly could approach your target, but we'd need to validate hit rates.
[09:24] Marta Alvarez: wow so caching is mission critical then.
[09:27] Alex Chen: yes — caching, tokenization optimizations, and moving high-cost workloads to scheduled batch reserved capacity are the three knobs most customers use.

[09:39] Priya Saini: can you talk through how Redwood reports token breakdown? we need per-route, per-token-type split for chargeback.
[09:46] Jordan Lee: Redwood Console has token-level breakdown by route/model and also shows cached vs generated tokens, per-request latency percentiles, and cost attribution. You can export CSVs for internal chargeback.

[09:59] Damian Huo: small random question — do you have any partner integrations with observability tools?
[10:03] Alex Chen: yes we integrate with datadog, splunk, and you can stream audit logs to your SIEM.

[10:10] Ethan Gray: okay, i want to circle back to the math — that example showed 10.9M tokens/day. if we keep 40k monthly budget we need to be orders of magnitude cheaper or have massive cache hits. what are realistic cache hit rates for similar customers?
[10:23] Samir Patel: in templated, high-repeat queries we've seen hit rates from 30% up to 70% depending on variability. for your route optimization where drivers repeat similar patterns, I'd expect mid-high 40s with some engineering on TTL and normalization. but we won't know until we run the shadow traffic test.

[10:45] Marta Alvarez: would you recommend starting on Hosted for speed, or jump to Dedicated to get unit econ?
[10:52] Alex Chen: if procurement is flexible, a Dedicated pilot is best because it gives you reliable latency and better cost signal. Hosted is faster to stand up and avoids commit, but you'll lose some predictability and may pay more per-token. Given your budget cap and need for SLOs, Dedicated pilot looks like the right call.

[11:10] Priya Saini: what about contract length for Dedicated? we have seasonal patterns so full-year commit might be risky.
[11:16] Samir Patel: we offer monthly reserved pools and annual discounts; there's also hybrid structures with minimums and overage at tiered rates so you can flex with seasonality. We'll include alternatives in the pilot proposal.

[11:30] Damien Huo: any red flags from your side given what we've shared?
[11:33] Jordan Lee: just to be sure we can meet the 99th pctl 250ms — that's achievable but requires tuning: right model selection, reserved capacity, and careful batching config. we'll validate in the benchmark.

[11:45] Ethan Gray: sounds fair. what's in the pilot deliverable?
[11:49] Alex Chen: deliverables: 1) benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 latencies and throughput, 2) token distribution and cache-hit analysis from shadow traffic, 3) projected monthly cost scenarios (hosted vs dedicated vs private), 4) regression checks on your summarization eval set, and 5) recommended rollout plan.

[12:12] Marta Alvarez: good. on compliance — we'll need SOC2 documents and a security whitepaper to share with our legal — can you send that?
[12:18] Samir Patel: yes we'll attach SOC2, data flow diagrams, and the security whitepaper. For Private deployments we'll also provide network architecture and KMS integration docs.

[12:29] Priya Saini: and can we get a sample SLA for Dedicated?
[12:33] Samir Patel: yes, we'll include SLA options in the pricing packet.

[12:40] Damien Huo: curious — any recommended short-term optimizations we can do before pilot to reduce initial burn? like prompt templating or token trimming?
[12:48] Jordan Lee: yes — normalize driver prompts, enforce strict system messages, trim unnecessary history, and move long-running summarizations to scheduled batch windows. We can share a short playbook.

[13:02] Samir Patel: ok last section — wrap and next steps. I'll recap: Samir to send pilot scope + pricing scenarios; Alex to run throughput benchmark and coordinate with Ethan for sample prompts; Jordan to prepare tokenization audit plan; Customer to confirm compliance recipients and timeline.
[13:20] Marta Alvarez: that's correct. thanks, this was very helpful.
[13:23] Ethan Gray: thanks all.
[13:25] Samir Patel: thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.
[13:30] Meeting end
